md: Segmentation limits how far one compromise spreads; zero trust removes network location as a reason to trust anything. Both assume a breach will happen, and both only pay off when someone watches the alerts at the boundaries.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: What TLS still reveals, and fingerprinting clients with JA3
md: A fingerprint identifies a TLS library and its configuration, not an intention. Python, Go and Windows programs share fingerprints with malware written in the same language or on the same stack. Use JA3 to cluster and to rank leads, never as a verdict on its own.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
md: Every packet is a header plus a payload. Every device on the path must read the header to deliver it, and can read the payload too unless it is encrypted. Both facts drive almost everything in network security.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
md: TLS protects the content of one connection between two endpoints. It does not hide who talks to whom, it does not make the server trustworthy, and it does not protect data once it is decrypted at either end.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
md: A detector outputs a variable-size set of (box, class, score) triples, and IoU between boxes is the measure every later stage builds on.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: Pick the counting method by scene: detection when objects are separable and you need locations, density maps for dense crowds where boxes fail, and tracking plus line or region events for video, where the same object appears in many frames.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
md: User programs run in ring 3 and can only ask; the kernel runs in ring 0 and decides. A system call is the only door between them. Sandboxing is mostly the art of closing doors and narrowing what each open door accepts.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Sandboxes: Chrome's broker model, macOS and iOS
md: A broker is only as good as its request checking. A broker that performs "open this path" for any path a renderer names has turned itself into a tool for the attacker. That failure has a name, the confused deputy, and it is the subject of lesson 15.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Your own footprint while investigating: OPSEC and bias
md: Investigating leaves traces. Use a separate, logged-out research environment, expect the other side to read its logs, and record your exact queries because results differ by engine, location and history.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
md: List clues, bound the area, eliminate candidates with the most distinctive clue first, then confirm with an independent feature. Report what matched and what could not be checked.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
md: An ethical OSINT engagement is authorised, planned, minimal, preserved, verified and reported with its limits, and it ends with fixes and deleted working data.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: CI is a contract written in the repo: on these events, on these machines, run these commands, and block the merge unless they exit with status 0. Read `.github/workflows/` before your first PR to a project.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Misconception: a reviewer who leaves 15 comments is blocking you on all 15. Often most are optional. If the reviewer did not say which ones block the merge, ask instead of guessing.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: Read in this order before you touch code: LICENSE (can you contribute at all), CONTRIBUTING (how), CODE_OF_CONDUCT (how to behave), SECURITY (if your finding is a vulnerability). Ten minutes of reading avoids a rejected PR.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebase rewrites history. The rule from Pro Git, the free Git book on git-scm.com: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Your own PR branch is the usual exception, which is why the next lesson's force-push needs care, not a ban.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: Public is not the same as open source. Code you can read on GitHub with no license file is all rights reserved, and so is a snippet whose license you never checked.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: CLA: one signed agreement per person or company, granting rights up front. DCO: no agreement, just a per-commit certification of origin via Signed-off-by, checked mechanically by email match.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
md: A common mistake is to fix a bug inside a generated file. Your edit is overwritten the next time the generator runs, and reviewers will reject it. When a file says *do not edit*, find its input (here `src/commands/get.json`) in the build rule and change that instead.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: Every cut is an experiment: remove, rerun, compare to the original failure. Keep cuts that preserve the exact error; undo the rest.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: If the project squash-merges PRs, your intermediate commits disappear from the main branch anyway, and the PR as a whole becomes one commit. That makes **one logical change per PR** even more important: the squash cannot separate a fix from a speedup after the fact.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths. It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: When authorisation is unclear: the Iowa courthouse arrests
md: Ambiguity is what got two professionals arrested. Write down: who owns each target, who signed for it, when testing may happen, who outside the client has been told, and two 24/7 ways to reach someone who can confirm it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
md: A sampling profiler answers one question: what fraction of CPU samples had this function on the stack? It is cheap because work happens per sample, not per call, and it is approximate because it is a sample.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Common misconception: "unflushed stores are lost on a crash." Some are, some are not, and the hardware chooses. Treat each dirty cache line as independently maybe-persisted. Flushes give you a lower bound on what is durable, never an upper bound.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works
md: Authentication checks answer "was this domain's use authorised?", never "is this message honest?". A display-name spoof or lookalike domain passes them cleanly. Defences need both: DMARC against exact-domain spoofing, and human-facing cues plus process rules for the rest.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Two rules give every struct layout: **each field's offset is a multiple of its alignment**, and **the struct's size is a multiple of its own alignment** (the largest field alignment). Everything else, including all the padding, follows from these.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A top-down pose model inherits every mistake of its detector. If two people overlap and NMS merges their boxes, or the detector misses someone, the keypoint network has no way to recover that person. The authors of OpenPose, the bottom-up system in lesson 3, call this **early commitment**: the pipeline commits to the detector's boxes before it has looked at a single joint.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
md: Misconception: "an algorithm is quantum-safe until someone builds a quantum computer that breaks it." Both 2022 breaks ran on ordinary computers. Confidence in ML-KEM and ML-DSA comes from years of public cryptanalysis of lattice problems, and NIST still hedged with HQC, which it says is based on different math than ML-KEM.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Post-filtering leaves the index untouched and is cheap when $s$ is large, but the result count is a random variable. To hold k results you must fetch on the order of $k/s$ candidates, and noticeably more for a high-probability guarantee.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Software prefetch: distance, hints and the kernel's lesson
md: **Rule:** add a software prefetch only where profiling shows misses, one site at a time, and keep it only if performance counters (hardware registers in the CPU that count events such as cache misses and prefetches, read with tools like perf) show useful prefetches and the timing improves. Drepper and the kernel developers reached the same conclusion from opposite results.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Location traces and aggregate maps: Strava 2018
md: "It's only aggregate data" fails when the crowd is small. A count of 25 is not one person, but it is 25 identifiable people at a place they did not mean to reveal.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: The Laplace mechanism: calibrating noise, worked
md: Laplace mechanism: add noise with scale sensitivity / epsilon. For counts that is 1 / epsilon, and 95 percent of answers fall within about 3 / epsilon of the truth. Every query spends epsilon from a finite budget.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Private set intersection: comparing lists without sharing them
md: PSI reveals set sizes and the intersection, and it cannot stop a party from choosing what goes into its own set. Cap sizes, rate-limit, and log query volumes per client to detect enumeration.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: After the foothold: the four tactics defenders must see
md: The foothold is rarely the disaster. Escalation, credential theft, discovery and lateral movement turn one infected laptop into a domain-wide incident, and each of them leaves evidence on the machines it touches.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: An ORM gets one label per solution and must discover where errors are. A PRM is told where the first error is. That extra information is why PRMs rank solutions better on hard problems, and why they can reject right answers reached by wrong reasoning.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: PRMs give denser, more precise feedback than outcome checks, but they are learned models: they can be exploited by search and RL, they degrade under distribution shift, and their labels (human, MC, or judge) each carry their own noise. Use them where search or reranking pays off and keep the final-answer verifier in the loop.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches
md: Misconception: "a context switch costs a few microseconds, so it does not matter." That is the direct cost on an idle cache. Li et al. found the total ranged from several microseconds to more than a thousand, depending on working set size and access pattern. Benchmarks that touch no data hide the part that hurts.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Prompt optimization is search: candidates (instructions and demos), a metric, a dev set to score on, and a proposer. Everything else in this course is a choice of proposer, a way to spend the budget, or a way to keep the final number honest.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: The funnel: from 100 backbones to a binder that works
md: More sampling buys you less than independence suggests. Sequence sampling cannot rescue an undesignable backbone, which is why designability of the generator, measured at a fixed small M, is the metric the backbone papers compete on.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: A hash match is strong evidence; a hash miss proves nothing. Security researcher David Bianco's [Pyramid of Pain](https://detect-respond.blogspot.com/2013/03/the-pyramid-of-pain.html) puts hash values at the bottom because changing a single byte gives the attacker a brand new hash. Use hash lists to catch known copies quickly, never as the only control.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
md: Misconception: expansion always helps. It helps when the added words mean the same thing **in this query's context**. *auto* means automobile in d6 but automatic in d9; a list that ignores sense trades recall for false matches. Here the bad synonym cost nothing at the top only because the good documents happened to score higher.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Sign bits only carry information if coordinates are spread around zero. Qdrant's docs say binary quantization needs a *centered distribution* of vector components. If every coordinate is positive, every bit is 1 and all vectors look identical; non-negative data such as SIFT (scale-invariant feature transform) image descriptors comes close to this. Lesson 2 measures this failure.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Prices, quantities and negative numbers: validating what input means
md: If a value influences price, access, ownership or state, assume the client made it up. Recompute it from server data, and validate every remaining input for business meaning: range, type, and how it combines with the other fields.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Flexcoin and Poloniex, the bitcoin banks that raced (2014)
md: Internal balances are money. A transfer between two users of the same service can drain the service if the debit is not atomic, because every later withdrawal trusts those balances.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
md: A concurrency test that passes once proves little: races are probabilistic. Use many parallel workers, a barrier so they start together, a real database rather than a mock, and run it on every build so a later refactor that reopens the window is caught.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory
md: RAG splits knowledge in two: the index decides **what facts are available**, the LLM decides **how they are read and phrased**. Every quality problem in this course is a failure of one of these two halves, or of the hand-off between them.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
md: Filling a missing value with 0 is safe only when 0 already means the worst value. For a feature like 1/window it does. For a z-scored feature, 0 means average, so a missing value silently becomes an average document. Use the worst observed value (LETOR's MIN approach) or add a separate is-missing flag.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: A crime with a supply chain: the roles and the money
md: Ransomware is a business whose only income is victims who pay. Every victim who can restore without paying lowers the expected value of the next intrusion, and every payment funds it.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Backups that survive an attacker with Domain Admin
md: A backup survives only if the credentials, network and storage that protect it are independent of production identity. Keep at least one copy immutable in a separate account or offline, back up AD and the rebuild tooling too, and time real restores.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: A short timeout detects dead peers fast but turns a transient congestion spike into a fatal QP error; a long one can stall an application for seconds. Pick it from your fabric's real round-trip and queueing delays, not from habit.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
md: Bandwidth is set by what changes, how it is encoded, and how often you send it. Latency under loss is set by the transport: an ordered stream turns one lost packet into a stall for every later update.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: A gap between a random-split number and a temporal-split number is not a bug in either; they measure different tasks. Only the temporal one resembles what the system will face, so compare models on that.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: Aggregation keeps a small state per group. Hashing finds the state with a table (memory grows with groups); sorting brings each group together so one state suffices (needs ordered input). Sort and hash nodes both spill to disk when they exceed their memory limit.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Concurrent writes, conflict resolution and what quorums do not promise
md: Pick the knobs by the question each one answers: **N** sets how many copies survive, **W** how many machines must hold a write before "ok", **R** how many you ask on a read, and **the conflict rule** decides what happens when copies disagree. Real configs: Dynamo's common (N, R, W) of (3, 2, 2); R = 1, W = N for read-heavy catalogs; Cassandra QUORUM with QUORUM.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
md: Misconception: verifiable rewards cannot be hacked. A verifier is only as strong as its isolation. If the agent can write to the tests, the test runner, the libraries they import, or read the reference answer, *pass the tests* and *solve the task* come apart.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: An auditor asking about risk management wants to see: a documented method (scales, appetite), a register with named owners, dated decisions by people with the authority to make them, and evidence that the register is reviewed on schedule. A register nobody reviews fails the audit even if every score is right.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: CSF 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; 22 categories, 106 subcategories; current and target profiles define your roadmap; tiers describe rigour. Voluntary, outcome-based and free, which makes it the common language between engineers, executives and other frameworks.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: EU law for engineers: GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act
md: Notification duties stack. One ransomware incident at a cloud provider in Germany can mean a GDPR notification to the data protection authority (72 hours), a NIS2 early warning to the CSIRT (24 hours), DORA reports via financial customers, and contractual notices to customers. Decide in advance who files which report; the clocks start whether or not you have a plan.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Accountability: what boards, CISOs and engineers have answered for
md: Red flags that should make any engineer escalate in writing: being asked to delete or delay logs, to describe an intrusion as "research", to pay an attacker through a bug bounty, to tell a regulator or customer something you know is false, or to keep the general counsel or board out of the loop. Follow your company's whistleblowing or escalation path; your own integrity is the control.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
md: Staleness is a dial, not a free lunch. Too tight a bound and the system stalls behind long trajectories again (AReaL notes small eta slows generation and recommends a large one); too loose and updates use data from much older policies, which prior work shows can degrade learning. Importance weights can also explode for tokens the behavior policy found unlikely, which is why verl truncates or rejects extreme ratios.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
md: Mitigating destroys evidence. Reverting the config drains the queue, restarts pods and rotates the logs that held the smoking gun. Before you revert, spend the 30 seconds: snapshot the pool metrics, grab one stack dump, copy the rendered config, note the exact timestamps. The chapter's phrase is that rapid triage does not preclude preserving evidence of what is going wrong.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Weighted RRF and multi-query fusion (RAG-Fusion)
md: Multi-query fusion has costs. In the Infineon study RAG-Fusion averaged 34.62 s versus 19.52 s for plain RAG (1.77 times slower in that deployment), mostly from the larger answer call, and some answers strayed off topic when the generated queries were not relevant enough. If the rewrites are near-duplicates, fusion just re-counts the same list.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Objects the C side owns: ARef, AlwaysRefCounted and RCU
md: Two ways to use an object you did not allocate: hold an `ARef<T>` when you need it to stay alive *across time* (stored in a struct, sent to another thread), or borrow it under an `rcu::Guard` when you only need it *briefly* and the data is RCU-protected. The first costs a refcount increment; the second costs almost nothing but forbids sleeping until the guard is dropped.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: Inserting a task into a local DSQ is a commitment. Once there, it waits for that CPU even if another CPU goes idle a microsecond later. Schedulers that want work sharing keep tasks in a shared custom DSQ and move them to a local DSQ only when a CPU asks via `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
md: Misconception: if no idle CPU was found, a busy CPU will pick the task up soon. Only CPUs that run their dispatch path do, and idle tracking races with CPUs going idle. Inserting into a queue no CPU will look at, with no kick, is how schedulers stall while CPUs idle.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Hard-coded credentials (CWE-798) and why deleting them fails
md: Environment variables are a stepping stone, not the goal. OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet warns that environment variables "are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps". Prefer files or APIs that the platform injects at runtime, readable only by the one process that needs them.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: What a secure code reviewer is looking for
md: A misconception: "the tests pass, so it is safe". Tests show the code does what was intended for the inputs someone thought of. A security review asks about inputs nobody thought of. Every bug in this course passed its author's tests.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Regular expressions that hang: ReDoS and the Cloudflare outage
md: Patterns written to *detect* attacks are code too. Cloudflare's outage came from a security rule, deployed globally within seconds because security rules must ship fast. Review regexes in WAF rules, input validators and log parsers with the same care as application code, and test them against long near-miss strings, not only against strings that match.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: what safe Rust promises, and reviewing unsafe
md: Review unsafe Rust as C, with one question: can any input from safe code make this block break its preconditions? Require a SAFETY comment that names the check, keep the block tiny, think about panics in the middle, and run the tests under Miri.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IKEv2: four messages to build the keys and the first tunnel
md: IKE_SA_INIT agrees on keys but proves nothing about who is on the other end; a man-in-the-middle could complete it. Authentication happens only in IKE_AUTH, where AUTH binds each peer's credential to the earlier messages. If AUTH is weak (a guessable pre-shared key), the whole tunnel is weak, however strong the Diffie-Hellman group.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
md: Architecture is placement. For each trust boundary, name the enforcement point, check that nothing can go around it, and list what it depends on. Those dependencies are your trusted computing base, and they deserve the most scrutiny.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: NIST SP 800-207: the logical architecture of zero trust
md: Zero trust concentrates trust in the policy engine, the administrator, the identity provider and the device inventory. Protect them as the most critical systems you run, and treat a change to access policy as a security event.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Queues: acknowledge fast, process later, expect duplicates
md: A longer visibility timeout reduces duplicates from slow workers. It never removes duplicates from storage redundancy or redelivery. The handler must be safe to run twice, whatever the queue settings.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: AI for finding bugs, reviewing code and writing detections
md: A rule that never fires looks exactly like a quiet network. Every detection, human or AI written, ships with samples it must match and samples it must not.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
md: "Zero-day" describes the defenders' situation (no fix existed), not how clever the attack is. Most real breaches use **known** vulnerabilities with patches available for weeks or years. Equifax (lesson 8) is the textbook example.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Defence in depth: layers, and why they must be independent
md: Defence in depth means several *different* layers across Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, so that one failure does not mean total failure. The math only works when layers fail independently: hunt down shared passwords, shared admin accounts and silent monitoring first.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Incident updates when you do not know yet
md: Never let an update outrun the evidence to sound reassuring. A confident claim that later proves wrong costs more trust than an honest "not yet known". The next lesson is a real case.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
md: A self-improvement loop is only as good as its filter. The precision of the check sets the quality of the kept data, and the set of problems the model can sometimes solve sets how far the loop can reach.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Evaluate compression like a model change: measure your task metric at several ratios on your own data, and measure end-to-end latency including the compressor. The published gains were measured on specific benchmarks with specific target models.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
md: Equifax, Spring4Shell, ProxyLogon (lesson 14) and MOVEit all ended the same way: a **web shell** written into a directory the web server executes. Two cheap controls hit all of them: make web roots read-only to the app's own user, and alert on new script files appearing there.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Prefix reuse is a property of the *whole serving path*: frontend hints, the radix tree, queue order on each worker, and routing across workers. Each layer can preserve reuse or destroy it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: Production routing = a graph from OSM (directed, with turn costs) + a preprocessing technique. CH gives the fastest queries on a fixed metric; partition-based MLD or CRP accepts new weights in seconds without redoing the expensive phase.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Two ceilings limit SIMD: latency chains (fix with several independent accumulators) and memory bandwidth (fix by doing more work per byte or keeping data in cache). Lane count only matters once both are out of the way.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: Bump allocation costs a few instructions and has no per-object free. It is ideal when a group of objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compiler pass) and wrong when objects die at unrelated times, because one long-lived object keeps the whole arena alive.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
md: A resumed partial sample can contain tokens generated by several weight versions. `--mask-offpolicy-in-partial-rollout` removes the old prefix tokens from the loss, but the docs note this does not remove the prefix-distribution mismatch: the newer tokens that are trained were still generated after a prefix the current policy might not have written.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
md: The CSRB's review of the group known as Lapsus$ found that, in a few cases, the attackers "impersonated help desk personnel over direct chat messages and encouraged employees to approve the MFA prompts". When you contact a user about an alert, use a channel the attacker cannot be sitting in, and teach users that the real SOC never asks them to approve a prompt.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics
md: The analyst's job, in one sentence: answer each alert with evidence, quickly and in order of risk, write it down so others can act and check, and use the access that makes this possible only for that purpose.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ
md: People outside your organisation (carrier staff, outsourced agents, contractors) can be the weak link for your accounts. Design so that no single outside person's mistake or bribe hands over a login, and make reporting approaches normal inside.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: Words to keep apart: a **latent** is a unit of the SAE; a **feature** is the concept you hope it captures. Gemma Scope says 'latents' for exactly this reason. A latent with a clean name is a hypothesis about a model feature, not proof of one.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Interpolation is not the same as smoothing. Most of these methods are *exact*: the surface passes through every reading. That is right for precise instruments and wrong for noisy cheap sensors, where you want a method that can treat part of each reading as measurement error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Choose interpolators by held-out error, not by reputation. Leave-one-out RMSE (or blocked cross-validation, which holds out whole regions so test points are not right next to training points) compares methods on your data, and the standardized errors tell you whether kriging's uncertainty can be trusted.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: A log-mel spectrogram is 80 numbers every 10 ms. Whisper's 30 second input is therefore an 80 x 3000 matrix: the model never sees raw samples.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The map of a process: segments, /proc/PID/maps and ASLR
md: A process is one sparse virtual address space: a handful of VMAs (code, data, bss, heap, mappings, libraries, stack, vdso), each with its own permissions and backing, separated by vast unmapped gaps, at addresses ASLR moves on every run.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
md: Read a pointer as five numbers: four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset. Huge pages simply end the walk early and widen the offset to 21 or 30 bits.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Directional ablation: erasing refusal from the residual stream
md: This is dual use. Removing a single direction strips the safety behavior from an open-weights chat model with minimal effect on other capabilities, which the authors read as evidence that current safety fine-tuning is brittle. They also show that adversarial suffixes (strings of tokens, found by automated search, appended to a harmful request to make the model comply) work partly by suppressing this same direction.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Online filtering: EMA as a low-pass, Welford for anomaly flags
md: Online operators keep O(1) state per key and update per reading. Mean and variance via Welford are order-independent; the EMA is not. Both are cheap enough to run per sensor in the stream processor.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Multi-head attention by hand: two heads, two patterns
md: Head A only *looks* like a previous-token head. It matches content: these four words happen to be distinct and in this order. Shuffle the sentence and it follows the words, not the positions. A real positional head needs the position information that Lesson 5 adds.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: Attention trades sequential steps for quadratic pairwise work. That is a great deal on GPUs for moderate n, and the reason long-context methods all target the n x n score matrix.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: `block_size` is the **maximum** context, not the only context. Because position $t$ in each chunk sees only $t+1$ tokens, the model is trained on every context length from 1 to `block_size`, which is exactly what it needs when generation starts from a short prompt.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
md: Training scores all positions in parallel with teacher forcing; generation is a sequential loop over the same network that samples from the last position's distribution, shaped by temperature, top-k or top-p.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: Steepest descent is a local statement. $-\nabla f(2, 1) = (-4, -6)$ does not point at the minimum $(0, 0)$, which lies in direction $(-2, -1)$. In an elongated bowl the gradient mostly points across the narrow valley, which is why plain gradient descent (repeatedly stepping against the gradient, lesson 6) zig-zags.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
md: `rm` and `mv` act at once and say nothing. `mv` onto an existing name silently replaces that file, and `rm -r` cannot be undone. Before deleting with a pattern, run `ls` with the same pattern to see what it matches, and add `-i` to make `rm` or `mv` ask first.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
md: A pipeline is several processes running concurrently and connected by bounded kernel buffers. Fast writers block on a full pipe; writers to a closed pipe get SIGPIPE. Tools like `sort` that need all their input are where a pipeline stops streaming.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
md: The private key works like your password on every server that lists its public key. Never copy it to a server or commit it to a repository, and protect it with a passphrase; `ssh-agent` can hold the unlocked key so you type the passphrase once per session.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying
md: An ID embedding is trained by whatever loss it feeds. Supervised losses place IDs with similar effects on the target close together. When the ID space is huge or open, trade exactness for a fixed-size table: hash, share an unknown row, or build vectors from features.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: Reserving the maximum length for every request wastes most of the cache. vLLM's profiling found only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory held actual token states in earlier systems, due to reserved slots and fragmentation. PagedAttention fixes this by allocating the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like OS pages.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Control flow is the program counter. Straight-line code advances it by the instruction length; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` overwrite it. A C `for` loop compiles to a compare plus a conditional jump backwards.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
md: Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of any single instruction. The flow breaks on dependencies on recent results and on jumps the predictor gets wrong; a misprediction costs roughly the pipeline's length in cycles.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT does not add much new knowledge. If the base model does not know a fact, a demonstration that states it mostly teaches the model to answer confidently in that style, which can increase made-up answers on other questions ([Gekhman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904)).

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of the documents that contain it. A query reads only the postings of its own terms, so the work depends on how common those terms are, not on how big the whole collection is.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: Production inverted indexes are sorted, gap-encoded and block-compressed, and are written once into immutable segments that get merged, not edited in place. The ranking formula on top is a replaceable component.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
md: A null pointer or an uninitialized pointer does not point to any object, and dereferencing it is *undefined behavior*: the C standard places no requirements on what happens. Often you get a crash (a segmentation fault on Linux: the process touched an address with no memory mapped there, so the operating system kills it), but the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, so do not rely on a crash to tell you.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Structs and linked data: ->, typedef and a linked list
md: Never touch a node after freeing it, and that includes reading its next field to continue a loop. Save every pointer you still need from a block before you free the block.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
md: On the Mac used for this course, the ASan runtime in Apple's clang refused leak detection: running with `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1` printed `detect_leaks is not supported on this platform`. On Linux, ASan's leak check is on by default. Check leaks where your tools support them, for example in Linux CI.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: The rule is not "only one reference to a variable per function". Sequential borrows are fine, as are many shared ones. The error only appears when a `&mut` borrow overlaps any other live borrow of the same value.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Closures and threads: moving ownership to another thread
md: A thread gets values by ownership: `move` them into its closure, `send` them through a channel, get them back from `join`. Since every value has one owner, two threads cannot both reach it unless a type built for sharing is in between.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
md: `A * B` in NumPy and PyTorch is the **element-wise** (Hadamard, after the mathematician Jacques Hadamard) product, which multiplies entries in matching positions, not matrix multiplication. Matrix multiplication is `A @ B` (or `np.matmul`). With two same-shape square matrices both run without error and give different answers, so this bug is silent.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
md: Tensors are arrays with any number of axes; `@` multiplies the last two and broadcasts the rest. Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, and sizes must be equal or 1. Name the axis a reduction removes, and keep it with `keepdims=True` when you broadcast back.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches: noisy gradients and the training loop
md: SGD steps on an unbiased but noisy gradient estimate from a minibatch. Noise falls only as $1/\sqrt B$, so moderate batches with many steps are usually the efficient choice.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Early stopping and why big models still generalize
md: Gradient descent fits high-curvature, smooth directions first and nearly flat, wiggly ones last. Noise lives mostly in the flat directions, so stopping at the best validation error keeps the signal and skips the noise. That is why early stopping acts like an L2 penalty.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
md: A ReLU hidden unit is a hinge (one input) or a cut with a ramp (many inputs). The output layer adds these up into a piecewise-linear function, and equivalently, it runs a linear model on the features the hidden layer computed.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Build it: a tiny autograd engine from scratch
md: Gradients accumulate across calls too. In this engine, `backward()` resets only the output's grad, so calling it twice on `f = x * x` with `x = 3` leaves `x.grad` at 12, not 6. That is why part 3 zeroes every parameter's grad before each backward pass, and why PyTorch training loops call `opt.zero_grad()`.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
md: A page fault is not a bug. It is a legal access to a page that happens not to be in memory, and the program never notices except as a delay. A segmentation fault is different: an access to an invalid page, which the OS treats as an error.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
md: Directories map names to inode numbers; inodes map file offsets to disk blocks; the per-process descriptor and the open file table remember where you are. Path lookup costs disk reads in proportion to the path's depth unless the cache has the blocks.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: The classic mistake is confusing $P(E \mid H)$ with $P(H \mid E)$, called base rate neglect. It shows up in ML with a classifier on a rare class. Its **recall** is $P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{positive class})$, the sensitivity, and does not depend on the base rate; its **precision** is $P(\text{positive class} \mid \text{flagged})$, the posterior, and does. High recall can still come with mostly false alarms.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
md: One matrix, Sigma, holds every pairwise covariance. Any weighted sum has variance a-transpose Sigma a, and a Gaussian with covariance Sigma is just mu + L z with independent standard normals z.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
md: Before launching, choose alpha, power and the minimum effect worth detecting, then compute n. Do not stop early on a peek unless the method allows it, and report the effect with its interval.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
md: Misconception: Kaplan's power laws were wrong. The loss-versus-size and loss-versus-data trends were real and still hold in shape. What shifted was the **compute-optimal allocation** derived from them, which is sensitive to experimental details. A scaling law is only as good as the runs it was fitted on.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests
md: By default trec_eval silently ignores queries for which a run retrieved nothing, so a system that crashes on hard queries can score higher. Pass -c to average over every query in the qrels, with missing queries scored 0.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Misconception: a higher similarity score means a more relevant passage across queries. Cosine scores are only comparable within one query's ranking and one model. A fixed threshold like 0.7 that works for one model can be meaningless for another.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
md: A byte-level BPE tokenizer is three small functions: train (count pairs, merge the top one, mint ids from 256), encode (apply merges by lowest id) and decode (join bytes, decode UTF-8 with errors replaced). The regex split adds one rule: count and merge inside chunks only.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Optimizers: momentum, Adam and decoupled weight decay
md: Adam's step is about **lr in size regardless of gradient scale**. That is its strength, and also why L2 regularization inside Adam misbehaves. Use AdamW when you want weight decay with an adaptive optimizer.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: Cosine similarity and inner product are not the same metric. If your embeddings are not unit-length, an inner-product index ranks differently from cosine. Faiss (Meta's open-source vector search library) documents the standard fix: normalize vectors to length 1. Cosine is the inner product divided by both lengths, so when both lengths are 1 the two are equal.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Install scripts: why installing a package runs its code
md: Blocking install scripts stops code that runs at install time. It does not stop malicious code that runs when your app imports the package, or a `.pth` file that Python runs on start-up. It removes the easiest path, not every path.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
md: Malicious dependency equals intrusion. Scope by version and time window, contain, assume every machine that ran it is compromised, rotate secrets from a clean machine, hunt, rebuild, then fix the control that failed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Verification is the fix: why filtered self-training does not collapse
md: The generator does not have to be right; the kept set has to be. Collapse is avoided when a verifier keeps more correct than incorrect examples, and its judgments must track this generator's actual errors.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
md: `mmap` signals failure with `MAP_FAILED`, which is `(void *) -1`, not `NULL`. Code that checks `if (p == NULL)` misses every error and later dereferences address -1.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: `MAP_FIXED` forcibly replaces whatever is already mapped at that address. In a multithreaded program another thread (or a library calling `dlopen`, which loads a shared library at run time, or `malloc`) may have just mapped something there, and you silently destroy it. mmap(2) recommends `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`, which fails with `EEXIST` (already exists) instead of clobbering.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: *Present* and a missing end date are not the same thing. *Present* is an explicit claim of a current role. A blank end date may mean the person forgot to fill it in. Pick a convention, store which case occurred, and do not silently treat blanks as current.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
md: Repeated sampling scales **coverage** smoothly; selection without a reliable checker does not keep up. The useful question is never only how many samples, but how good is the verifier at the tail.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Sequential thinking lets later tokens build on earlier ones, which parallel sampling cannot. s1 found that majority voting over the base model could not catch up with the budget-forced fine-tuned model.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
md: Every number here is one group's runs at 760M parameters or less. A later public reimplementation (lesson 8) found the full model did not always beat its baselines, while the memory itself consistently helped over attention-only variants.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
md: Every modern malloc fast path is the same idea as the 2001 magazine layer: a small, private stack of free objects per thread or CPU, refilled and drained in batches from a locked shared layer, with sizing policies to cap the memory that sits idle.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
md: Measure a hunt programme by what it changes: detections created, gaps and vulnerabilities closed, techniques examined, and the dwell time of anything it finds. Intrusions found matter most when they happen, but a quarter without one is not a failed quarter if the organisation is harder to attack at the end of it.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames
md: Use the kill chain to ask "where can we act against this adversary, and how many independent ways?" and ATT&CK to ask "which of their known behaviours can we see?". Both answer defender decisions, which is why they belong in intelligence products.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack surface: every door, window and vent
md: "Internal only" is not off the surface. An endpoint reachable only from inside the network is still reachable by anyone who gets inside: a phished employee, a compromised vendor login, a malicious insider. Count it, and protect it as if the network were hostile.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Third-party access is a trust boundary you do not fully control. Give each vendor the narrowest path, watch it closely, and assume the vendor's own computers may already be compromised.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A forecast is a prediction made at an origin $T$ using only data up to $T$, for a stated horizon $h$. Every evaluation in this course respects that constraint.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Reading an X.509 certificate field by field
md: Common misconception: "the CN must match the hostname". Modern clients ignore CN for name matching and check SAN only; a certificate with the right CN but no matching SAN entry fails in browsers and in Python's ssl module.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
md: `tl.load` with a mask but no `other=` leaves masked lanes **undefined**. That is safe only if those lanes never feed a result. Any reduction (sum, max) over a masked block needs `other=` set to the operation's neutral value: the value that leaves the result unchanged, 0 for a sum (x + 0 = x) and minus infinity for a max (max(x, -inf) = x).

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
md: Misconception: "lambda is just a weight, any value works." Text cross-entropy and noise MSE live on different scales, and lambda decides how the shared weights split their capacity. Transfusion used 5, BAGEL effectively 4 (0.25 CE + 1 MSE is a quarter of CE + 4 MSE). Change the noise parameterization or schedule and the right value moves.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
md: Build-time specialization = **pick components by configuration, link statically, let DCE and LTO remove the rest**. Reconfiguring means rebuilding.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
md: At hundreds of dimensions, a distance does about 0.5 to 0.75 FLOPs per byte of vector it reads. SIMD makes the arithmetic cheap; after that, the bytes you move (and the cache misses you take) decide the speed.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Turning on mmap does not shrink an index; it only lets the OS evict parts of it. If the hot working set does not fit, latency can fall off a cliff, because each miss is a disk read instead of a DRAM access.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
md: Video cost is **frames x tokens per frame**. Every long-video method attacks one factor: fewer frames (sampling), fewer tokens per frame (pooling), fewer tokens over time (merging, memory), a bigger budget (long context), or a different representation (text captions).

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
md: A ViT-B/16 backbone is 85.8M parameters, 99% of them in 12 identical blocks of 7.09M each, and two thirds of each block is MLP. The classification head is tiny: 77,669 parameters for 101 classes.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
md: Misconception: web pretraining teaches the robot new motions. It does not. Web knowledge helps decide *which* object and *where*; the motor skills themselves still come from robot demonstrations.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: FSQ and LFQ: quantizers with no learned codebook
md: FSQ and LFQ trade a learned codebook for a fixed grid. You lose the freedom to place codes where the data is dense, and gain full usage by construction, no codebook loss, and vocabularies of 2^16 to 2^18 that VQ struggles to use.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades
md: CUDA graphs constrain attention through shape (pad to a captured size), address (persistent metadata buffers) and kernel choice (`AttentionCGSupport`). The weakest backend in the model sets the graph mode for everyone.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
md: A high benchmark score does not mean the model looked at the image. The BlindTest paper cites prior work finding that 42.9% of MMMU questions can be answered without the image. Build a small eval from your own documents, with the image-free baseline as a control.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
md: Check every layer. A wait-free algorithm is only as wait-free as its primitives and helpers: a `fetch_or` that compiles to a CAS loop, an allocator that takes a lock, or a reclamation scheme that can block will each reintroduce unbounded waiting.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Web testing as work: pentests, disclosure programmes and bounties
md: A pentest buys coverage of an agreed scope; a bug bounty buys the first valid report of each root cause; a VDP buys reports without payment. In all three the written rules, published or signed before testing, are what make the work legal.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: File inclusion: when a path parameter chooses the code that runs
md: Path traversal reads a file; file inclusion runs it. The fix for both is the same idea: the user picks from a list the server owns, never a path.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Origins and sites: how the browser names who owns a page
md: Same-site is not same-origin. `login.example.com` and `blog.example.com` are same-site but cross-origin. A weak subdomain (an old blog, a marketing page run by a vendor) is "same-site" with your login page, and cookie rules and SameSite (lesson 5) treat it as a friend.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Site isolation: separate processes as a second wall
md: Site isolation is **defence in depth** for the browser itself. It does not change what web pages are allowed to do, so it will not stop XSS, CSRF or a bad CORS policy. It limits the damage when the browser's own enforcement fails.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: SMB file shares and EternalBlue: how WannaCry spread
md: Worms need two things: a reachable service and a bug in it. Patching removes the bug; turning off SMBv1 and blocking 445 removes the reachability. Do both, because you will never patch everything on time.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Public Wi-Fi and captive portals in the HTTPS era
md: On public Wi-Fi, TLS with correct certificate validation is what protects you, not the Wi-Fi layer. The risks that remain are the places where TLS is missing (first HTTP request, portal page) or broken (apps that skip validation).

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Misconception: more workers always means more throughput. With one locked queue, past the knee extra workers only add waiters on the same lock and the same cache line. The model here is deliberately simple, but the cap of 1/c is real for any serial section.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
md: WSD is **not fully schedule-free**. Optimal peak LR still shifts with training length: Bergsma et al. (2025) quote Shen et al. puzzling that the best WSD LRs differ by token count, and Hägele et al. found the best cooldown peak LR was about half the best cosine peak. Tune the peak LR at roughly the length you care about; lesson 7 gives the evidence and a rule for adjusting it.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
md: Writing into a buffer before its id completes does not crash anything, but it corrupts your own stream: the modified bytes may go out on the wire or in a retransmission. The kernel docs: kernel integrity is not affected, but a buggy program can corrupt its own data stream.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
md: Zero-shot replaces training data with design choices. Make those choices on a labeled dev set: compare templates or descriptions, pick argmax or per-label thresholds by the cost of errors, and re-check whenever the labels change.
